title: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: V \propto L^{1/2} for swimming (Froude), flight (minimum speed) and walking (pendulum leg)

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the general result, attained under very different conditions and arrived at by very different modes of reasoning, is in every case that the velocity tends to vary as the square root of the linear dimensions of the organism.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Speed in locomotion”. Scope: swimming, flying and walking animals of similar construction

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: V \propto L^{1/2} for swimming (Froude), flight (minimum speed) and walking (pendulum leg)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The exponent is directly estimable with standard allometric models, and large open movement and trait resources exist. Coverage and standardization are uneven across all three modes, and the similar-construction condition reduces effective sample size.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within each locomotor mode and among similarly constructed species, regress characteristic velocity on linear size and test whether the exponent is 0.5. Mode-specific exponents significantly different from one-half would refute the claimed common result.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Characteristic speed must be standardized across tracking studies.

Construction, behavior and environment covary strongly with size.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.9
data existence: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The shared square-root prediction is precise and could be distinguished from other exponents with size-matched speeds. Open tracking and fisheries databases contain speeds and lengths, but not the three theoretical speeds the derivations name, and similar construction is hard to enforce. A careful subset analysis is feasible; it would not settle all three modes together.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit log speed on log length separately for swimming, flight, and walking among animals of similar construction. An exponent near one-half in each case would support the claim; exponents near zero or one would favor the obvious rivals.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Tracked speeds are mostly routine movement, not minimum flight speed, sprint speed, or pendulum walking speed.

Cross-species samples mix mechanical design with the size effect the claim sets aside.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.5
